claim: Khoomei is a unique singing style originating from the republic of Tuva in central Asia.
source: Khoomei is a unique singing style originating from the republic of Tuva in central Asia.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is established knowledge about Khoomei.

claim: Khoomei singers produce two pitches simultaneously: a booming low-frequency rumble alongside a hovering high-pitched whistle-like tone.
source: Singers produce two pitches simultaneously: a booming low-frequency rumble alongside a hovering high-pitched whistle-like tone.
evidence: This is a direct description of the acoustic phenomenon and is supported by the audio analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tuvan singers show remarkable control in shaping their vocal tract to narrowly focus the harmonics (or overtones) emanating from their vocal cords.
source: Tuvan singers show remarkable control in shaping their vocal tract to narrowly focus the harmonics (or overtones) emanating from their vocal cords.
evidence: This is supported by the MRI data and computational modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The biphonic sound is a combination of the fundamental pitch and a focused filter state at 1–2 kHz formed by merging two formants.
source: The biphonic sound is a combination of the fundamental pitch and a focused filter state, which is at the higher pitch (1–2 kHz) and formed by merging two formants, thereby greatly enhancing sound-production in a very narrow frequency range.
evidence: This is supported by spectral analysis and computational modeling showing formant merging.

claim: Biphonation in Khoomei arises from linear filtering rather than from a nonlinear source.
source: Most importantly, we demonstrate that this biphonation is a phenomenon arising from linear filtering rather than from a nonlinear source.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling and analysis of the harmonic structure.

claim: Richard Feynman was attempting to visit Tuva in the years preceding his death.
source: In the years preceding his death, Richard Feynman had been attempting to visit the small republic of Tuva located in geographic center of Asia (Leighton, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leighton, 2000.

claim: Kip Thorne gifted Feynman a record called Melody tuvy featuring Tuvan singing in Khoomei style.
source: A key catalyst came from Kip Thorne, who had gifted him a record called Melody tuvy, featuring a Tuvan singing in a style known as Khoomei, or Xöömij.
evidence: This is stated as a historical fact in the introduction.

claim: Feynman was never successful in visiting Tuva.
source: Although he was never successful in visiting Tuva, Feynman was nonetheless captivated by Khoomei, which can be best described as a high-pitched tone, similar to a whistle carrying a melody, hovering above a constant booming low-frequency rumble.
evidence: This is stated as a historical fact.

claim: Khoomei is now part of the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
source: Khoomei, now a part of the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, is characterized as "the simultaneous performance by one singer of a held pitch in the lower register and a melody … in the higher register" (Aksenov, 1973).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about UNESCO recognition.

claim: Khoomei is characterized as the simultaneous performance by one singer of a held pitch in the lower register and a melody in the higher register.
source: Khoomei, now a part of the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, is characterized as "the simultaneous performance by one singer of a held pitch in the lower register and a melody … in the higher register" (Aksenov, 1973).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aksenov, 1973.

claim: The biophysical underpinnings of biphonic human vocal style are not fully understood.
source: Even today, the biophysical underpinnings of this biphonic human vocal style are not fully understood.
evidence: This is stated as motivation for the study.

claim: The vocal tract acts as a spectral filter that sculpts the sound emanating from the vocal folds.
source: Upon emanating from the vocal folds, they are then sculpted by the vocal tract, which acts as a spectral filter.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vocal production.

claim: The vocal-tract filter has multiple resonances that accentuate certain clusters of overtones, creating formants.
source: The vocal-tract filter has multiple resonances that accentuate certain clusters of overtones, creating formants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vocal acoustics.

claim: When speaking, we change the shape of our vocal tract to shift formants in systematic ways characteristic of vowel and consonant sounds.
source: When speaking, we change the shape of our vocal tract to shift formants in systematic ways characteristic of vowel and consonant sounds.
evidence: This is established knowledge about speech production.

claim: Singing largely uses vowel-like sounds.
source: Indeed, singing largely uses vowel-like sounds (Story, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Story, 2016.

claim: Two possible loci for the biphonic property in Khoomei are the source and/or the filter.
source: Two possible loci for this biphonic property are the source and/or the filter.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis to be tested.

claim: Birds can produce multiple notes that are harmonically unrelated using two vibrating nonlinear sound sources in the syrinx.
source: A source-based explanation could involve different mechanisms, such as two vibrating nonlinear sound sources in the syrinx of birds, which produce multiple notes that are harmonically unrelated (Fee et al., 1998; Zollinger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fee et al., 1998 and Zollinger et al., 2008.

claim: Humans are generally considered to have only a single sound source, the vocal folds.
source: Humans however are generally considered to have only a single source, the vocal folds.
evidence: This is established knowledge about human vocal anatomy.

claim: Aerodynamic instabilities are known to produce biphonation.
source: For example, aerodynamic instabilities are known to produce biphonation (Mahrt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mahrt et al., 2016.

claim: Khoomei often involves dramatic and sudden transitions from simple tonal singing to biophonation.
source: Further, Khoomei often involves dramatic and sudden transitions from simple tonal singing to biophonation (see Figure 1 and the Appendix for associated audio samples).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1 and audio samples.

claim: Abrupt changes are often considered hallmarks of physiological nonlinearity.
source: Such abrupt changes are often considered hallmarks of physiological nonlinearity (Goldberger et al., 2002), and vocal production can generally be nonlinear in nature (Herzel and Reuter, 1996; Mergell and Herzel, 1997; Fitch et al., 2002; Suthers et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Vocal production can generally be nonlinear in nature.
source: Such abrupt changes are often considered hallmarks of physiological nonlinearity (Goldberger et al., 2002), and vocal production can generally be nonlinear in nature (Herzel and Reuter, 1996; Mergell and Herzel, 1997; Fitch et al., 2002; Suthers et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: It remains possible that biphonation arises from nonlinear source considerations.
source: Therefore it remains possible that biphonation arises from nonlinear source considerations.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility based on prior literature.

claim: Levin and Edgerton examined a wide variety of Tuvan throat singing song types and suggested three components at play.
source: In one seminal study of Tuvan throat singing, Levin and Edgerton examined a wide variety of song types and suggested that there were three components at play.
evidence: This is a reference to prior work, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: Levin and Edgerton suggested that narrowing of the formant appeared crucial to Khoomei production.
source: The first two ('tuning a harmonic' relative to the filter and lengthening the closed phase of the vocal fold vibration) represented a coupling between source and filter. But it was the third, narrowing of the formant, that appeared crucial.
evidence: This is a description of prior work by Levin and Edgerton.

claim: Levin and Edgerton offered little empirical justification for how vocal tract shape produces the effects they described.
source: Yet, the authors offered little empirical justification for how these effects are produced by the vocal tract shape in the presented radiographs.
evidence: This is a critique of prior work.

claim: It remains unclear how the high-pitched formant in Khoomei was formed.
source: Thus it remains unclear how the high-pitched formant in Khoomei was formed (Grawunder, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grawunder, 2009.

claim: Adachi and Yamada examined a throat singer using MRI and captured static images of the vocal tract shape during singing.
source: Another study (Adachi and Yamada, 1999) examined a throat singer using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and captured static images of the vocal tract shape during singing.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adachi and Yamada, 1999.

claim: Adachi and Yamada argued that a 'rear cavity' was formed in the vocal tract and its resonance was essential to biphonation.
source: Adachi and Yamada argued that a "rear cavity" was formed in the vocal tract and its resonance was essential to biphonation.
evidence: This is a description of prior work by Adachi and Yamada.

claim: Adachi and Yamada's MRI data reveal limited detail since they were static images of singers already in the biphonation state.
source: However, their MRI data reveal limited detail since they were static images of singers already in the biphonation state.
evidence: This is a critique of prior work.

claim: Small variations in vocal tract geometry can have pronounced effects on produced song.
source: Small variations in vocal tract geometry can have pronounced effects on produced song (Story et al., 1996) and data from static MRI would reveal little about how and which parts of the vocal tract change shape as the singers transition from simple tonal song to biphonation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Story et al., 1996.

claim: Data from static MRI would reveal little about how and which parts of the vocal tract change shape during transitions from tonal to biphonic singing.
source: Small variations in vocal tract geometry can have pronounced effects on produced song (Story et al., 1996) and data from static MRI would reveal little about how and which parts of the vocal tract change shape as the singers transition from simple tonal song to biphonation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of static imaging.

claim: A dynamic description of vocal tract morphology is required to understand which features are crucial to biophonation.
source: To understand which features of vocal tract morphology are crucial to biophonation, a dynamic description of vocal tract morphology would be required.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the study design.

claim: The study uses MRI to acquire volumetric 3D shape of the vocal tract of a singer during biphonation.
source: We use MRI to acquire volumetric 3D shape of the vocal tract of a singer during biphonation.
evidence: This describes the methods used in the study.

claim: The study captures dynamic changes in a midsagittal slice of the vocal tract as singers transition from tonal to biphonic singing.
source: Then, we capture the dynamic changes in a midsagittal slice of the vocal tract as singers transition from tonal to biphonic singing while making simultaneous audio recordings of the song.
evidence: This describes the methods used in the study.

claim: The study uses a computational model to gain insight into which features of vocal tract morphology are responsible for biphonic Khoomei song.
source: We use these empirical data to guide our use of a computational model, which allows us to gain insight into which features of vocal tract morphology are responsible for the singing phonetics observed during biophonic Khoomei song (e.g., Story, 2016).
evidence: This describes the methods used in the study.

claim: The study focuses specifically on the Sygyt (or Sigit) style of Khoomei.
source: We focus specifically on the Sygyt (or Sigit) style of Khoomei (Aksenov, 1973).
evidence: This describes the scope of the study.

claim: Measurements were made from three Tuvan singers performing Khoomei in the Sygyt style (designated as T1–T3) and one (T4) in a non-Sygyt style.
source: We made measurements from three Tuvan singers performing Khoomei in the Sygyt style (designated as T1–T3) and one (T4) in a non-Sygyt style.
evidence: This describes the study participants.

claim: Varying degrees of vibrato can be observed in the singers, dependent upon the singer.
source: Varying degrees of vibrato can be observed, dependent upon the singer (Figure 1; see also longer spectrograms in Appendix 1—figure 6 and Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: This is observed in the spectrograms.

claim: Singer T4 performing in a non-Sygyt style exhibited a fundamental frequency of approximately 130 Hz.
source: In contrast to these three singers, singer T4 performing in a non-Sygyt style exhibited a fundamental frequency of approximately 130 Hz, although significant energy additionally appears around 50–55 Hz, well below an expected subharmonic (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This is measured from the audio recordings.

claim: Singer T4 shows significant energy around 50–55 Hz, well below an expected subharmonic.
source: In contrast to these three singers, singer T4 performing in a non-Sygyt style exhibited a fundamental frequency of approximately 130 Hz, although significant energy additionally appears around 50–55 Hz, well below an expected subharmonic (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: This is observed in the spectral analysis.

claim: As the singers transition from normal singing to biphonation, the formant structure changes significantly and the positions of formant peaks shift dramatically and rapidly.
source: As the singers transition from normal singing to biphonation, we see that the formant structure changes significantly and the positions of formant peaks shift dramatically and rapidly.
evidence: This is observed in the spectral analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Once in the biphonation mode, all three singers demonstrate overtones in a narrow spectral band around 1.5–2 kHz.
source: Once in the biphonation mode, all three singers demonstrate overtones in a narrow spectral band around 1.5–2 kHz; we refer to this as the focused state.
evidence: This is observed in the spectral analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the focused state, ±1 overtones are as much 15–35 dB below the central overtone.
source: Specifically, Figure 1 shows that not only is just a single or small group of overtones accentuated, but also that nearby ones are greatly attenuated: ±1 overtones are as much 15–35 dB and ±2 overtones are 35–65 dB below the central overtone.
evidence: This is measured from the spectral data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the focused state, ±2 overtones are 35–65 dB below the central overtone.
source: Specifically, Figure 1 shows that not only is just a single or small group of overtones accentuated, but also that nearby ones are greatly attenuated: ±1 overtones are as much 15–35 dB and ±2 overtones are 35–65 dB below the central overtone.
evidence: This is measured from the spectral data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The energy in the low-frequency region associated with the first formant (below 500 Hz) is roughly constant between the normal-singing and focused states.
source: Whereas the energy in the low-frequency region associated with the first formant (below 500 Hz) is roughly constant between the normal-singing and focused states, there is a dramatic change in the spectrum for the higher formants above 500 Hz.
evidence: This is observed in the spectral analysis.

claim: There is a dramatic change in the spectrum for the higher formants above 500 Hz between normal singing and the focused state.
source: Whereas the energy in the low-frequency region associated with the first formant (below 500 Hz) is roughly constant between the normal-singing and focused states, there is a dramatic change in the spectrum for the higher formants above 500 Hz.
evidence: This is observed in the spectral analysis.

claim: In normal singing, spectral energy is distributed across several formants between 500 and 4000 Hz.
source: In normal singing (i.e., prior to the focused state), spectral energy is distributed across several formants between 500 and 4000 Hz.
evidence: This is observed in the spectral analysis.

claim: In the focused state, the energy above 500 Hz becomes narrowly focused in the 1.5–2 kHz region.
source: In the focused state after the transition, the energy above 500 Hz becomes narrowly focused in the 1.5–2 kHz region, generating a whistle-like pitch that carries the song melody.
evidence: This is observed in the spectral analysis.

claim: The focused state generates a whistle-like pitch that carries the song melody.
source: In the focused state after the transition, the energy above 500 Hz becomes narrowly focused in the 1.5–2 kHz region, generating a whistle-like pitch that carries the song melody.
evidence: This is observed in the audio and spectral analysis.

claim: Once the transition into the focused state occurs, eR(1,2) values are large (upwards of 0.5 and higher) and sustained across time.
source: However once the transition occurs (red triangle in Figure 1), those values are large (upwards of 0.5 and higher) and sustained across time (Appendix 1—figure 2 and Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is measured from the audio recordings and shown in the appendix figures.

claim: Singer T2 created multiple focused formants.
source: For one of the singers (T2) the situation was more complex, as he created multiple focused formants (Figure 1 middle panels and Appendix 1—figure 6, Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This is observed in the spectral analysis.

claim: Singer T2's second focused state was not explicitly dependent upon the first.
source: The second focused state was not explicitly dependent upon the first: The first focused state clearly moves and transitions between approximately 1.5–2 kHz (by 30%) while the second focused state remains constant at approximately 3–3.5 kHz (changing less than 1%).
evidence: This is observed in the spectral analysis.

claim: The focused states in singer T2 are not harmonically related.
source: Thus the focused states are not harmonically related.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the two focused states move independently.

claim: Singer T2 had more energy in the higher overtones compared to the other singers.
source: Unlike the other singers, T2 not only has a second focused state, but also had more energy in the higher overtones (Figure 1).
evidence: This is observed in the spectral analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The transition into the focused state is fast (∼40–60 ms).
source: This transition into the focused state is fast (∼40–60 ms), as are the shorter transitions within the focused state where the singer melodically changes the filter that forms the whistle-like component of their song (Figure 1, Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This is measured from the audio recordings.

claim: The transitions within the focused state where the singer melodically changes the filter are fast.
source: This transition into the focused state is fast (∼40–60 ms), as are the shorter transitions within the focused state where the singer melodically changes the filter that forms the whistle-like component of their song (Figure 1, Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This is measured from the audio recordings.

claim: The working hypothesis was that vocal tract shape determines the formants in Khoomei.
source: The working hypothesis was that vocal tract shape determines these formants.
evidence: This is stated as the hypothesis being tested.

claim: The study obtained two types of MRI data: steady-state volumetric data and dynamic midsagittal images.
source: First, there are two types of MRI data reported here: steady-state volumetric data Figure 3 and Appendix 1—figure 18) and dynamic midsagittal images at several frames per second that capture changes in vocal tract position (Figure 4A–B and Appendix 1—figure 20).
evidence: This describes the methods used in the study.

claim: The dynamic MRI data allow examination of vocal tract changes as song transitions into a focused state.
source: Second is that the dynamic data allow us to examine vocal tract changes as song transitions into a focused state (e.g., Appendix 1—figure 20).
evidence: This describes the capability of the methods used.

claim: The human vocal tract begins at the vocal folds and ends at the lips.
source: The human vocal tract begins at the vocal folds and ends at the lips.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Airflow produced by the vocal cords sets the air-column in the tract into vibration, and its acoustics determine the sound that emanates from the mouth.
source: Airflow produced by the vocal cords sets the air-column in the tract into vibration, and its acoustics determine the sound that emanates from the mouth.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vocal production.

claim: The vocal tract is effectively a tube-like cavity whose shape can be altered by several articulators: the jaw, lips, tongue, velum, epiglottis, larynx and trachea.
source: The vocal tract is effectively a tube-like cavity whose shape can be altered by several articulators: the jaw, lips, tongue, velum, epiglottis, larynx and trachea (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Producing speech or song requires that the shape of the vocal tract, and hence its acoustics, are precisely controlled.
source: Producing speech or song requires that the shape of the vocal tract, and hence its acoustics, are precisely controlled (Story, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Story, 2016.

claim: There are two distinct and relevant constrictions in the vocal tract during Khoomei production, corresponding roughly to the uvula and alveolar ridge.
source: The most important feature however, is that there are two distinct and relevant constrictions when in the focused state, corresponding roughly to the uvula and alveolar ridge.
evidence: This is observed in the MRI data.

claim: The vocal tract is expanded in the region just anterior to the alveolar ridge during Khoomei.
source: Additionally, the vocal tract is expanded in the region just anterior to the alveolar ridge (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is observed in the MRI data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The retroflex position of the tongue tip and blade produces a constriction at 14 cm and results in the opening of a sublingual space.
source: The retroflex position of the tongue tip and blade produces a constriction at 14 cm, and also results in the opening of this sublingual space.
evidence: This is observed in the MRI data.

claim: The degree of constriction at the two locations (uvula and alveolar ridge) is hypothesized to be the primary mechanism for creating and controlling the frequency at which the formant is focused.
source: It is the degree of constriction at these two locations that is hypothesized to be the primary mechanism for creating and controlling the frequency at which the formant is focused.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the MRI observations.

claim: The modeling approach uses a well-established linear 'source/filter' model.
source: Our approach was to use a well-established linear "source/filter" model (e.g., Stevens, 2000) that includes known energy losses (Sondhi and Schroeter, 1987; Story et al., 2000; Story, 2013).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach and cites supporting literature.

claim: The system is assumed to behave linearly, allowing for a simple multiplicative relationship between the source and filter in the spectral domain.
source: We begin with a first order assumption that the system behaves linearly, which allows us for a simple multiplicative relationship between the source and filter in the spectral domain (e.g., Appendix 1—figure 10).
evidence: This describes the modeling assumptions.

claim: Acoustic characteristics of the vocal tract can be captured by transforming the three-dimensional configuration into a tube with variation in its cross-sectional area from the glottis to the lips.
source: Acoustic characteristics of the vocal tract can be captured by transforming the three-dimensional configuration (Figure 3) into a tube with variation in its cross-sectional area from the glottis to the lips (Figure 4 and Figure 5).
evidence: This describes the modeling approach.

claim: The representation of the vocal tract shape as variation in cross-sectional area is called an area function.
source: This representation of the vocal tract shape is called an area function, and allows for calculation of the corresponding frequency response function (from which the formant frequencies can be determined) with a one-dimensional wave propagation algorithm.
evidence: This is a definition from established terminology.

claim: The area function allows for calculation of the corresponding frequency response function with a one-dimensional wave propagation algorithm.
source: This representation of the vocal tract shape is called an area function, and allows for calculation of the corresponding frequency response function (from which the formant frequencies can be determined) with a one-dimensional wave propagation algorithm.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach.

claim: The 3D reconstructions of the Tuvan singer's vocal tract were affected by a large shadow from a dental post.
source: Although the area function can be obtained directly from a 3D vocal tract reconstruction (e.g., Story et al., 1996), the 3D reconstructions of the Tuvan singer's vocal tract were affected by a large shadow from a dental post (e.g., see Figure 4) and were not amenable to detailed measurements of cross-sectional area.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the data.

claim: A cross-sectional area function was measured from the midsagittal slice of the 3D image set.
source: Instead, a cross-sectional area function was measured from the midsagittal slice of the 3D image set (see Materials and methods and Appendix for details).
evidence: This describes the method used to overcome the limitation.

claim: The MRI data provided crucial bounds for model parameters: the locations of primary constrictions and thereby the associated area functions.
source: Thus, the MRI data provided crucial bounds for model parameters: the locations of primary constrictions and thereby the associated area functions.
evidence: This describes how the MRI data informed the model.

claim: The merging of F₂ and F₃ could be useful for effectively amplifying a specific overtone, making it a prominent acoustic feature in Khoomei.
source: We hypothesize that this mechanism could be useful for effectively amplifying a specific overtone, such that it becomes a prominent acoustic feature in the sound produced by a singer, specifically the high frequency component of Khoomei.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the modeling results.

claim: While the singers are in the normal song mode, there are no obvious strong constrictions in their vocal tracts.
source: While the singers are in the normal song mode, there are no obvious strong constrictions in their vocal tracts (e.g., Appendix 1—figure 11).
evidence: This is observed in the MRI data.

claim: After the singers transition to the focused state, a strong constriction near the alveolar ridge is observed in each MRI.
source: After they transition, in each MRI from the focused state, we observe a strong constriction near the alveolar ridge.
evidence: This is observed in the MRI data.

claim: A constriction near the uvula in the upper pharynx is observed in the focused state, but the degree of constriction varies.
source: We also observe a constriction near the uvula in the upper pharynx, but the degree of constriction here varies.
evidence: This is observed in the MRI data.

claim: Variations in the constriction near the uvula are co-variant with the frequency of the focused formant.
source: If we examine the simultaneous audio recordings, we find that variations in this constriction are co-variant with the frequency of the focused formant.
evidence: This is observed by comparing MRI and audio data.

claim: A dynamic implementation of the model reasonably captures the rapid transition into/out of the focused state.
source: Further, a dynamic implementation of the model, as shown in Appendix 1—figure 14, reasonably captures the rapid transition into/out of the focused state as shown in Figure 1.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the modeling results.

claim: The model confirms and explains how articulatory changes give rise to the observed acoustic effects.
source: Taken together, the model confirms and explains how these articulatory changes give rise to the observed acoustic effects.
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results.

claim: An overtone singer could potentially 'play' various harmonics by first generating a tight constriction in the oral cavity near the alveolar ridge.
source: To summarize, an overtone singer could potentially 'play' (i.e., select) various harmonics of the voice source by first generating a tight constriction in the oral cavity near the alveolar ridge, and then modulating the degree of constriction in the uvular region of the upper pharynx to vary the position of the focused formant, thereby generating a basis for melodic structure.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanism inferred from the study.

claim: An overtone singer modulates the degree of constriction in the uvular region of the upper pharynx to vary the position of the focused formant, thereby generating a basis for melodic structure.
source: To summarize, an overtone singer could potentially 'play' (i.e., select) various harmonics of the voice source by first generating a tight constriction in the oral cavity near the alveolar ridge, and then modulating the degree of constriction in the uvular region of the upper pharynx to vary the position of the focused formant, thereby generating a basis for melodic structure.
evidence: This is a summary of the mechanism inferred from the study.

claim: Tuvan singers performing Sygyt-style Khoomei exercise precise control of the vocal tract to effectively merge multiple formants together.
source: This study has shown that Tuvan singers performing Sygyt-style Khoomei exercise precise control of the vocal tract to effectively merge multiple formants together.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Tuvan singers morph their vocal tracts to create a sustained focused state that effectively filters an underlying stable array of overtones.
source: They morph their vocal tracts so to create a sustained focused state that effectively filters an underlying stable array of overtones.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding.

claim: Some singers are capable of producing additional foci at higher frequencies.
source: Some singers are even capable of producing additional foci at higher frequencies.
evidence: This is observed in the data from singer T2.

claim: A linear framework (source/filter model) appears sufficient to capture the behavior of Khoomei including the sudden transitions into a focused state.
source: Below, we argue that a linear framework (i.e., source/filter model, Stevens, 2000) appears sufficient to capture this behavior including the sudden transitions into a focused state, demonstrating that nonlinearities are not a priori essential.
evidence: This is argued based on the modeling results.

claim: Nonlinearities are not a priori essential for producing Khoomei.
source: Below, we argue that a linear framework (i.e., source/filter model, Stevens, 2000) appears sufficient to capture this behavior including the sudden transitions into a focused state, demonstrating that nonlinearities are not a priori essential.
evidence: This is argued based on the modeling results.

claim: Since the filter characteristics are highly sensitive to vocal tract geometry, precise biomechanical motor control of the singers is sufficient to achieve a focused state without invoking nonlinearities or a second source.
source: That is, since the filter characteristics are highly sensitive to vocal tract geometry, precise biomechanical motor control of the singers is sufficient to achieve a focused state without invoking nonlinearities or a second source as found in other vocalization types (e.g., Herzel and Reuter, 1996; Fee et al., 1998).
evidence: This is argued based on the modeling results and comparison to other vocalization types.

claim: The notion of a focused state is mostly consistent with vocal tract filter-based explanations for biphonation in previous studies.
source: The notion of a focused state is mostly consistent with vocal tract filter-based explanations for biphonation in previous studies (e.g., Bloothooft et al., 1992; Edgerton et al., 1999; Adachi and Yamada, 1999; Grawunder, 2009), where terms such as an 'interaction of closely spaced formants', 'reinforced harmonics', and 'formant melting' were used.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature.

claim: The present results are broadly consistent with Adachi and Yamada (1999) in that a constricted 'rear cavity' is crucial.
source: Our results explain how this occurs and are also broadly consistent with Adachi and Yamada (1999) in that a constricted 'rear cavity' is crucial.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work.

claim: The present data appear inconsistent with conclusions from previous studies of Khoomei that center on effects arising from changes in the source.
source: Further, the present data appear in several ways inconsistent with conclusions from previous studies of Khoomei, especially those that center on effects that arise from changes in the source.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work.

claim: The overtone structure is highly stable, though some vibrato may be present.
source: First, we observed overtone structure to be highly stable, though some vibrato may be present.
evidence: This is observed in the spectral analysis.

claim: The stability of the overtone structure argues against a transition into a different mode of glottal pulse generation, which could allow for a 'second source'.
source: Further, this stability argues against a transition into a different mode of glottal pulse generation, which could allow for a 'second source' (Mergell and Herzel, 1997).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, with reference to prior work.

claim: A single sharply defined harmonic alone is not sufficient to get the salient perception of a focused state.
source: Second, a single sharply defined harmonic alone is not sufficient to get the salient perception of a focused state, as had been suggested by Levin and Edgerton (1999).
evidence: This is argued based on observations in the data.

claim: Pressed phonation occurs when glottal flow is affected by tightening the laryngeal muscles such that the ventricular folds are brought into vibration.
source: Pressed phonation, also referred to as ventricular voice, occurs when glottal flow is affected by virtue of tightening the laryngeal muscles such that the ventricular folds are brought into vibration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about phonation types.

claim: Pressed phonation has the perceptual effect of adding a degree of roughness to the voice sound.

claim: The results provide context for how human song production and perception may be similar and/or different relative to that of non-humans.
source: Connecting back to nonlinear phonation mechanisms in non-mammals, our results provide further context for how human song production and perception may be similar and/or different relative to that of non-humans (e.g., Doolittle et al., 2014; Kingsley et al., 2018).

claim: Features that appear transiently in spectrograms provide hints of source nonlinearity, such as the brief appearance of subharmonics in some instances.
source: Nevertheless, features that appear transiently in spectrograms do provide hints of source nonlinearity, such as the brief appearance of subharmonics in some instances (Appendix 1—figure 15B).
evidence: This is observed in the spectrograms.

claim: Further analysis of Khoomei audio recordings may help to inform the model and might better capture focused filter sharpness and the origin of secondary focused states.
source: We suggest that further analysis (e.g., Theiler et al., 1992; Tokuda et al., 2002; Kantz and Schreiber, 2004) of Khoomei audio recordings may help to inform the model and might better capture focused filter sharpness and the origin of secondary focused states.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work.

claim: The spectro-temporal signatures of biphonic Khoomei raise questions about how they create the classical perception of Sygyt-style Khoomei as two distinct sounds.
source: Although this study did not directly assess the percept associated with these vocal productions, the results raise pressing questions about how the spectro-temporal signatures of biphonic Khoomei described here create the classical perception of Sygyt-style Khoomei as two distinct sounds (Aksenov, 1973).
evidence: This is a discussion of perceptual implications.

claim: The high-pitched melody is present only during the focused-state intervals and probably reflects a pitch associated with the focused formant.
source: The second sound, the high-pitched melody, is present only during the focused-state intervals and probably reflects a pitch associated with the focused formant.
evidence: This is an inference about pitch perception.

claim: The auditory system tends to group together concurrent harmonics into a single perceived object with a common pitch.
source: The auditory system tends to group together concurrent harmonics into a single perceived object with a common pitch (Roberts et al., 2015), and the multiple formants of a sung or unsung voice are not generally perceived as separate sounds from the low harmonics.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roberts et al., 2015.

claim: The multiple formants of a sung or unsung voice are not generally perceived as separate sounds from the low harmonics.
source: The auditory system tends to group together concurrent harmonics into a single perceived object with a common pitch (Roberts et al., 2015), and the multiple formants of a sung or unsung voice are not generally perceived as separate sounds from the low harmonics.
evidence: This is established knowledge about auditory perception.

claim: The fact that the focused formant is so narrow apparently leads the auditory system to interpret this sound as if it were a separate tone, independent of the low harmonics.
source: The fact that the focused formant is so narrow apparently leads the auditory system to interpret this sound as if it were a separate tone, independent of the low harmonics associated with the drone percept, thereby effectively leading to a pitch decoherence.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about perceptual mechanisms.

claim: The perceptual separation of the focused formant could be attributable to a combination of both bottom-up (cochlear) and top-down (perceptual) factors.
source: This perceptual separation could be attributable to a combination of both bottom-up (i.e., cochlear) and top-down (i.e., perceptual) factors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about perceptual mechanisms.

claim: The formant will be represented as a single spectral peak, similar to the representation of a single pure tone at the formant frequency.
source: Instead, the formant will be represented as a single spectral peak, similar to the representation of a single pure tone at the formant frequency.

claim: Other top-down mechanisms of auditory-object formation may play a more important role in generating a perception of two separate objects in Khoomei.
source: Rather, other top-down mechanisms of auditory-object formation may play a more important role in generating a perception of two separate objects in Khoomei.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about perceptual mechanisms.

claim: The rapid onsets of the focused formant may enhance its perceptual separation from the constant drone.
source: For example, the rapid onsets of the focused formant may enhance its perceptual separation from the constant drone (Darwin, 1984).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Darwin, 1984.

claim: FM differences between harmonic sounds generally have little influence on their perceived separation.
source: Although it has been argued that FM differences between harmonic sounds generally have little influence on their perceived separation (Darwin, 2005), others have reported enhanced separation in the special case in which one complex was static and the other had applied FM (Summerfield and Culling, 1992) – similar to the first and second formants during the Tuvan focused state.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Darwin, 2005.

claim: Enhanced separation has been reported in the special case in which one complex was static and the other had applied FM.
source: Although it has been argued that FM differences between harmonic sounds generally have little influence on their perceived separation (Darwin, 2005), others have reported enhanced separation in the special case in which one complex was static and the other had applied FM (Summerfield and Culling, 1992) – similar to the first and second formants during the Tuvan focused state.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Summerfield and Culling, 1992.

claim: The perceptual separation of the two sounds in Tuvan song might be further affected by a priori expectations about the spectral qualities of vocal formants.
source: The perceptual separation of the two sounds in the Tuvan song might be further affected by a priori expectations about the spectral qualities of vocal formants (Billig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Billig et al., 2013.

claim: Because a narrow formant occurs so rarely in natural singing and speech, the auditory system might be pre-disposed against perceiving it as a phonetic element.
source: Because a narrow formant occurs so rarely in natural singing and speech, the auditory system might be pre-disposed against perceiving it as a phonetic element, limiting its perceptual integration with the other existing formants.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about perceptual mechanisms.

claim: When three or four individual frequency-modulated sinusoids are presented at formant frequencies in lieu of natural formants, listeners can, with sufficient training, perceive the combination as speech.
source: When three or four individual frequency-modulated sinusoids are presented at formant frequencies in lieu of natural formants, listeners can, with sufficient training, perceive the combination as speech (Remez et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Remez et al., 1981.

claim: Listeners largely perceive sine-wave speech individual pure tones as separate auditory objects.
source: Nevertheless, listeners largely perceive these unnatural individual pure tones as separate auditory objects (Remez et al., 2001), much like the focused formant in Khoomei.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Remez et al., 2001.
